failure.message: The visual review found 6 serious problems with how the scene is drawn or computed. You have not been charged. It was corrected automatically twice, but it still did not pass. Revise plan prepares a simpler plan from your request for you to review, using up to 56 AI credits; nothing is built until you press Generate.

plan.title: Gradient descent: a ball stepping down a loss surface
plan.description: A curved loss surface with contour lines holds a ball, with an arrow under it pointing straight downhill. Each step moves the ball downhill by the learning rate times the slope, and a trail marks every point it has visited. You can take one step at a time or let the steps run, drag the ball to a new starting point, and change the learning rate to see small careful steps, zig-zagging, or steps so big the ball shoots off the surface.
plan.reason: Watching one step at a time while you change the learning rate and the starting point shows how gradient descent decides each move, and when it settles, zig-zags, gets stuck or blows up.

options.label: Two valleys (a shallow and a deep one)

interactions: Take one step: the ball moves once along the downhill arrow and the trail grows by one point
Let the steps run on their own, and pause them, with the card's step controls
Drag the ball to choose where it starts; this clears the trail and the step count
Change the learning rate: small values take many tiny steps, larger ones zig-zag across the bowl, and above about 0.67 the ball overshoots more each step until it leaves the bowl
Switch the surface shape: on the two-valley surface, where the ball ends up depends on where it starts, and it can stop in the shallow valley
assumptions: This is an illustration: the surface is a made-up formula, not the loss of a real trained model.

The bowl is loss = 0.5·(x² + 3y²): steeper in one direction than the other, so the learning rate it can handle depends on direction (above 2/3 it overshoots further on every step along the steep direction).
The two-valley surface is a smooth made-up formula with a shallow valley and a deeper valley, so it has a nearby trap (a local minimum) and the true lowest point (the global minimum).
Each step uses the exact slope of the formula: new position = old position − learning rate × slope. There is no randomness, no momentum and no friction.
Readouts show the step count, the loss at the ball, and the steepness (the size of the slope) at the ball.
Stepping stops when the steepness falls below 0.001 (the ball has settled), after 200 steps, or when the ball leaves the edge of the drawn surface; a readout says which one happened.
The trail draws one marker every 2 steps, at most 100 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
The ball jumps from point to point, one step at a time. It does not roll with speed or momentum like a real ball, because plain gradient descent has no momentum.
The surface has two inputs so it can be drawn. Real models have millions, and their loss cannot be seen as a surface.
The arrow shows the downhill direction (opposite the slope), and its length grows with the steepness. It is not drawn to the same scale as the step the ball actually takes.
Loss can rise on a step when the learning rate is large. Steps are not guaranteed to improve, and the readout shows this when it happens.
plan.learningGoal: Gradient descent repeatedly moves against the slope by a learning-rate-sized amount. Too small is slow, too large zig-zags or diverges, and where you start can decide which valley you end in.

draft.title: Gradient descent: a ball stepping down a loss surface
draft.description: A curved loss surface with contour lines holds a red ball. A dark arrow at the ball points straight downhill, and it is longer where the surface is steeper. Each step moves the ball by the learning rate times the slope. An orange trail marks where it has been. You can step once, run or pause the steps, drag the ball left or right to pick a new start, change the learning rate, or switch to a surface with a shallow valley and a deep valley.

options.label: Two valleys (a shallow and a deep one)

assumptions: This is an illustration: the surface is a made-up formula, not the loss of a real trained model.

Bowl: loss = 0.5·(x² + 3y²), where the plan's y is the depth direction z. It is steeper along z, so a learning rate above 2/3 overshoots further on each step along z until the ball leaves the surface.
Two valleys: loss = 0.25x⁴ − x² + 0.3x + 1.5 + 0.75y². The shallow valley is near x = 1.32, where the loss is about 0.91. The deep valley is near x = −1.48, where it is about 0.07.
Each step: new position = old position − learning rate × exact slope. No noise, momentum or friction. Steps run about 10 per second. Height is drawn at 0.4 × loss.
Stopping: steepness below 0.001 (converged), 200 steps reached, or the ball outside the drawn square |x|, |y| ≤ 2 (diverged). The loss can rise on a step; the Loss change readout shows this.
The arrow points downhill, opposite the slope; its length is 0.2 × the steepness, not the step size. Its label hides when the arrow is short (steepness below 1.5).
Dragging moves the starting point left or right only (x). The start always uses y = 1.3. Dragging or switching the surface clears the trail and the step count.
The trail marks the start and every step, up to 201 points (all 200 steps). The heights on the surface are rounded to 0.01.

findings.message: The default camera at (4.6,4.8,5.6) looks almost straight down the bowl's steep z direction. The bowl looks like a narrow U taking up about 40% of the frame width, with a lot of empty space around it. The area where the ball descends is squeezed into a few dozen pixels near the bottom (compare the side view, where the elliptical contours and the start point are easy to read). Move the default came

The plan says the learner drags the ball to choose the start point. The artifact only allows dragging along x and fixes z at 1.3. This is disclosed, but it limits starting points on the bowl. Behaviour on the two-valley surface and at learning rate 0.01 was not sampled.

In the default view the 27-step path appears as a short orange stub about 40 px long at the bottom of the bowl. The camera angle hides the z component of the descent, so the learner can't follow the steps (the side view shows a clear curve). This is the same camera problem as in the initial capture.

Near the minimum the steepness is 0.125, so the arrow is 0.025 long and can't be seen. The 'Downhill' label still sits on the ball, labelling nothing and looking larger than what it names. Hide the label (or the arrow and label together) when the arrow is too short to see. Don't give the arrow a minimum length.
The Status text readout ('running') does not appear in the readout strip, so the promised stop reason can't be seen in the capture.
The ball has left the surface (z=2.55) and the host draws it clamped at y=3.2, not its true 3.46. The Status readout 'diverged' does not show in the readout strip.
The 'Downhill' label floats over the ball even though the arrow has shrunk to almost nothing (length 0.025). The label names an object that can't be seen. Hide it when the arrow is too short to see.
The trail segments are straight chords between points, and the first segment looks thin and partly hidden where it crosses near the surface.

The plan says a readout tells the learner why stepping stopped (converged, 200 steps or diverged). The trace has a 'status' readout, but the readout bar in every capture shows only loss, steps, steepness and loss change. The status never appears on screen. Show it, for example as a numeric or coded readout, or as a scene label near the ball.

The plan's limitation says the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps. The artifact draws all 201 points and says so in its assumptions. This differs from the plan but is disclosed, and it is harmless.

Not sampled: the two-valley surface, dragging the ball, the low learning-rate end (0.01) and the toggle that hides the arrow. Dragging works along x only (the start always uses y = 1.3). That is disclosed, but it is narrower than the plan's 'drag the ball to choose where it starts'.
The status readout (here 'running') is computed but missing from the readout bar, so the learner cannot see whether the run is going, paused or settled.

At learning rate 0.8 the ball diverges after 2 steps. The loss is 9.7405, which checks out against the formula. But the 'diverged' status is not shown anywhere in the capture, so the learner gets no stopping reason, which the plan promises.
The ball's drawn height is capped at 3.6 by min(0.4·loss, 3.6), but 0.4 × 9.74 = 3.90. Its height therefore no longer matches the loss readout, and the cap is not disclosed.
The trail segment from the first step to the second is drawn as a near-hairline, while the other segments are thick.
The status readout is missing from the readout bar (same problem as in the default view).
The status readout is missing from the readout bar (same problem as in the default view).
The 'diverged' status is not shown, so the learner sees a ball floating off the surface with no stated reason why stepping stopped.
